content: 1. Cephalexin can increase the levels or effects of metolazone due to competition for renal tubular clearance with acidic (anionic) drugs. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown but considered minor. 2. Cephalexin reduces the efficacy of oral microbiota products by pharmacodynamic antagonism. These products contain bacterial spores, and co-administration with antibacterial agents may decrease their effectiveness. It is recommended to complete antibiotic regimens 2-4 days before initiating oral microbiota therapy. 3. Cephalexin can increase the levels or effects of mycophenolate by competing for renal tubular clearance with acidic (anionic) drugs. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 4. Cephalexin may increase the levels or effects of nabumetone, naproxen, oxaprozin, parecoxib, piroxicam, salicylates (non-ASA), salsalate, sulindac, tolfenamic acid, and tolmetin due to competition for renal tubular clearance with acidic (anionic) drugs. These interactions are considered minor, and their clinical significance is unknown. 5. Cephalexin can increase the toxicity of neomycin, plazomicin, streptomycin, and tobramycin due to nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity. Cephalosporins may enhance the nephrotoxic effects of aminoglycosides. Caution and close monitoring are recommended. 6. Cephalexin decreases the effects of nivolumab, pembrolizumab, penpulimab, retifanlimab, sintilimab, tislelizumab, and toripalimab through an unspecified interaction mechanism. Co-administration may interfere with the therapeutic effects of immune checkpoint inhibitors. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 7. Cephalexin decreases the levels or effects of pantothenic acid, pyridoxine, thiamine, and sodium picosulfate/magnesium oxide/anhydrous citric acid by altering intestinal flora. These interactions apply only to the oral forms of both agents and are considered minor with unknown clinical significance. 8. Cephalexin reduces the efficacy of live typhoid vaccine due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. Live bacterial vaccines should not be administered until antibiotic therapy is completed. This interaction is serious, and alternative approaches are recommended. 9. Cephalexin increases the levels or effects of valacyclovir and valganciclovir by competing for renal tubular clearance with acidic (anionic) drugs. The clinical significance of these interactions is unknown but considered minor. 10. Cephalexin and temocillin may increase each other's levels by decreasing renal clearance. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 11. Cephalexin increases the effects of warfarin through an unspecified interaction mechanism. Caution and close monitoring are recommended. 12. Zinc decreases the levels or effects of cephalexin by cation binding in the gastrointestinal tract. It is recommended to administer oral zinc salts at least 3 hours after cephalexin. Therapy modification and close monitoring are advised. 13. Cephalexin may cause various adverse effects, including abdominal pain, agitation, anemia, angioedema, confusion, diarrhea, dizziness, dyspepsia, elevated transaminases, eosinophilia, hemolytic anemia, epidermal necrolysis, erythema multiforme, fatigue, gastritis, genital pruritus, hallucinations, headache, hypersensitivity, nephritis, neutropenia, pseudomembranous colitis, thrombocytopenia, transient hepatitis, toxic epidermal necrolysis, urticaria, vaginal discharge, and vomiting. 14. Cephalexin is appropriate for endocarditis prophylaxis only in high-risk patients, as per American Heart Association guidelines. 15. Dose adjustments are necessary in severe renal insufficiency, as high doses may cause central nervous system toxicity. 16. Prolonged use or repeated therapy with cephalexin may lead to superinfections and the promotion of non-susceptible organisms. 17. Prolonged treatment, hepatic or renal disease, or nutritional deficiency may increase the international normalized ratio (INR). 18. Prolonged use of cephalexin is associated with fungal or bacterial superinfections. 19. Cephalexin should be used with caution in patients with a history of hypersensitivity to penicillin. 20. There are no adequate and well-controlled studies on cephalexin use in pregnant women. Available epidemiologic data and pharmacovigilance case reports over several decades have not established drug-associated risks of major birth defects, miscarriage, or adverse maternal or fetal outcomes. 21. Cephalexin is present in human milk, with a relative infant dose (RID) of less than 1% of the maternal weight-adjusted dose. There are no data on its effects on breastfed children or milk production. The benefits of breastfeeding should be weighed against the mother's clinical need for therapy and any potential adverse effects on the breastfed child. 22. Cephalexin is generally considered acceptable during pregnancy, as controlled studies in pregnant women show no evidence of fetal risk. 23. Cephalexin is excreted primarily in urine (80-100% as unchanged drug) within 2 hours. 24. The above information is provided for general informational and educational purposes only.
